classification.reason: FTT teaching episode from subtitle extraction

problem.title_as_question: Why does your forehand keep disappearing, and how do you build a repeatable, controllable stroke?
problem.definition: Players lose control and consistency on their forehand because they lack proximal stability in the hips, trunk, and shoulder blade, forcing the arm and hand to make unstable upper body compensations.
prerequisites: Players attempting to generate topspin or power on their forehand but suffering from intermittent loss of control and ball shanking.

symptoms.description: Sudden loss of ball control or spraying balls long to the back fence even at slow swing speeds.
Torso popping up and over-rotating around through the stroke instead of maintaining posture.
Falling backward, to the left, or to the right on follow-through instead of finishing balanced over the front foot.
Contacting the ball too close to the body, crowding the swing and forcing an arm-push.
Racket sliding, micro-twisting, or lacking stable sensory connection in the palm during stroke.

causes.statement: Hips extending forward in front of the shoulders with knees forward and chest up (quad dominant posture) rather than maintaining a hip hinge.
Intentionally driving the pelvis open forward instead of rotating the upper body over a stable pelvic base.
Loading weight onto the inside heel / over-pronated flat foot rather than loading the arch and ball of the foot.
Failing to transfer weight cleanly onto the front foot anchor at finish.
Upper trapezius shrugging and lack of isometric engagement in the mid-traps and serratus anterior, detaching the hitting arm from the trunk.
Positioning too close laterally to the ball, blocking the natural swing lane created by trunk flexion.
Gripping too loosely (0/10) or with gaps between the handle and palm, causing the racket to twist upon contact.

angles.summary: Explosive throwing mechanics in the arm only function when rooted in proximal stability at the hip-trunk connection and the scapula-shoulder interface.
Stabilizing the hip and upper body mimics a Romanian deadlift position where the butt stays back and the chest stays forward throughout the swing.
The hitting elbow should be visualized as tracing a smooth, gentle semicircle along the surface of a table supported by back engagement.
Players often try to intentionally pop their hips forward or keep their grip completely loose (0/10), which actually destroys control and leads to popping up and twisting.
The hand acts as a sensory organ communicating upstream balance and timing, while the large muscles of the trunk and hips provide the physical driving force for the hitting arm.

solutions.summary: Exaggerate keeping butt back, chest forward, and knees relatively straight with back flat through the entire swing, rotating the spine and trunk over anchored hips.
Set hips sideways and imagine only turning the upper body without intentionally rotating the pelvis; allow the back hip to contribute only intuitively.
Feel the range of knee motion over the foot, ensuring weight is rolled over the arch and outside of the ball of the foot rather than collapsing onto the inside heel.
Glide weight smoothly onto the front foot and hold a completely balanced finish over that front foot without falling backward or sideways.
Undo any upper trap shrugging, activate isometric tone in the mid-traps and serratus to attach the shoulder down, and swing the elbow along an imaginary table.
solutions.external_goal: Swing the elbow along the surface of an imaginary table

solutions.summary: Position further away from the ball laterally to allow the racket to swing freely through the natural lane established by the hinged trunk posture.
solutions.external_goal: Keep the ball pushed farther away laterally to the side into the natural swinging lane

solutions.summary: Push racket firmly into palm/V with non-dominant hand, eliminate grip gaps to maximize skin-to-handle contact, and raise tension to 5-6/10 if losing control so the racket cannot twist independently.
